title: The “IT support” caller — question explanation
learningObjective: Verify caller identity and resist verbal pressure to disclose data or approve actions
format: 16:9 educational motion-graphics video; narration; separate captions; no autoplay with sound
visualStyle: Deep navy and charcoal; restrained cyan/electric-blue highlights; limited purple accents; clean typography; purposeful, low-motion transitions; accessible contrast.

scenes.name: Scenario setup
scenes.visual: A caller claiming to be IT support says your laptop is infected and asks you to install a remote-access tool and read out an authentication code.
scenes.direction: Show a fictional simulated setting. Use generic UI and no actual organization, brand, user identity, credential, real URL or live account.

scenes.name: Learning objective and risk cue
scenes.visual: Verify caller identity and resist verbal pressure to disclose data or approve actions
scenes.direction: Highlight only observable cues and explain the decision context without implying certainty beyond the scenario.

scenes.name: Recommended response
scenes.visual: Option C: End the call and contact IT using the organization’s published helpdesk route. Independently verify support requests; never disclose authentication outputs to an unsolicited caller.
scenes.direction: Animate the recommended defensive choice as a clear decision path. Display the action verb and trusted channel/control.

scenes.name: Why the other options fail
scenes.visual: Option A: The code may authorize account access even without remote-control software. Option B: Unverified remote access can give the caller control of the device. Option D: A photo can be fabricated or copied and is not reliable identity verification.
scenes.direction: Show each unsafe alternative separately with a complete, concise reason. Do not depict operational exploitation, malicious code or credential capture.

scenes.name: Defensive takeaway
scenes.visual: End the call. Contact the helpdesk using a known directory or portal and report the attempted remote-access and code request. Caller ID, technical language and urgency are not proof that a caller is authorized.
scenes.direction: Close with one readable takeaway and the next safe action. Keep the final frame long enough for comprehension.
scenes.onScreenText: Caller ID, technical language and urgency are not proof that a caller is authorized.

Option D is unsafe because A photo can be fabricated or copied and is not reliable identity verification. In practice: End the call. Contact the helpdesk using a known directory or portal and report the attempted remote-access and code request. Key takeaway: Caller ID, technical language and urgency are not proof that a caller is authorized.
